analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every American comprehensive health insurance coverage through federally funded state programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, no other senator signed on, and it died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given states federal money to set up their own programs covering every resident, using the same benefit package that members of Congress' own health plan offers. Poorer families would have paid little or nothing; employers would have had to keep paying most premiums. A second phase would have required every state to reach 100 percent coverage by 2006, with competitive bidding among health plans and new patient-safety and worker protections.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 45 million uninsured Americans named in the bill's findings, plus low- and moderate-income families who would face capped premiums and cost-sharing, and health care workers who would get notice, staffing, and rehire protections.

how_it_helps.text: States could receive unlimited federal funds to build systems covering all residents, with benefits at least equal to the Federal Employees Health Benefits standard Blue Cross/Blue Shield preferred provider option [S2].

Families below 150 percent of poverty would pay no premium and at most 0.5 percent of income in cost-sharing; families between 150 and 300 percent of poverty would have premiums and cost-sharing capped at 3 and 5 percent of income [S3].

Preexisting condition exclusions would be banned under the plans, and every state would have to reach 100 percent coverage of eligible residents by January 1, 2006, with residents allowed to sue states that fail [S3].

Employers with fewer than 500 employees would have to contribute at least 80 percent of premiums (capped at 10 percent of wages), and larger employers would either match that or cover workers directly [S3].

The bill would cap insurer administrative costs — at least 90 percent of premium income must go to actual care within two years — require annual competitive bidding, and would remove ERISA preemption so state rules on health plans could be enforced [S3].
It would add full mental health and substance-abuse parity to Medicare and fold the patient-protection provisions of two House bills into federal law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose overhead and margin under the administrative-cost cap and annual bidding; employers would bear new or continued premium contributions; and the bill stated the cost should be offset by budget surpluses and reductions in tax benefits for top-bracket individuals and large corporations.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriated 'such sums as may be necessary' in permanent budget authority with no dollar estimate in the text, so the federal cost was unpriced; the offset provision was only a nonbinding sense of Congress [S3].

Phase I left the design to each state and gave the Secretary broad waiver authority, so coverage, quality, and cost control would have varied widely from state to state and depended on state capacity [S3].

Employers would have faced new contribution mandates capped at 10 percent of employee wages, a real cost for small and mid-sized businesses, and states would have had to police maintenance-of-effort rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — universal coverage for 45 million uninsured people at protected benefit levels — is very large, and the bill's own findings point to administrative savings of roughly $800 per person compared with other universal systems. But the financing was left open-ended and unpriced, and the two-phase, state-by-state structure with broad waivers would have made results uneven. It was an ambitious but incomplete blueprint, and it never advanced far enough for those costs to be debated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the Health Security for All Americans Act on July 19, 2000, and delivered introductory remarks [S5].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; no hearing, markup, or vote is listed in the action history [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after additional introductory remarks on July 25, 2000, and the Congress ended January 3, 2001 with the bill still in committee [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, health insurers kept the existing market structure and overhead, employers faced no new contribution mandates, and the 45 million uninsured gained nothing; no member of Congress was ever recorded voting on it.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks, and referred it to committee; it had no other Senate sponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 19, 2000 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a second sponsor from either party, so there was no record of party support or opposition beyond the referral.

industries.note: The bill would cap administrative overhead at 10-15 percent of premiums, force annual competitive bidding, and strip ERISA preemption, shrinking insurers' overhead and profit pool even though most coverage would still flow through qualified private plans.

Employers would have to fund at least 80 percent of employee premiums (capped at 10 percent of wages) or cover workers directly, though large firms paying above-poverty wages could choose their own route. This is a real cost, in exchange for the shared benefit of a universally covered workforce.

The bill's nonbinding offset provision called for paying for the program partly by cutting 'unnecessary Federal tax benefits available only to individuals and large corporations' in the maximum tax brackets.

industries.industry: Health care workers and their unions
industries.note: The bill includes staffing standards research, advance notice of closures and mergers, a right of first refusal for displaced workers, and a ban on using federal funds to influence unionization votes.
